opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It was actually a fairly natural transition, though at the time it felt like a big leap.

During my PhD I worked on physics-based character animation: making simulated characters swim, walk, or ride a bike by optimizing controllers inside a physics simulator. What I loved was that you don't hand-key the motion. You describe the body, the physics, and the goal, and the movement emerges from optimization. Over time, though, I kept running into the same nagging feeling. In graphics, success means it *looks* right. If the character's feet slide a bit, or the simulator is too forgiving, nobody really cares as long as the animation is convincing. I wanted the motion to actually *work*.

Robotics was the obvious place to test that. A robot is the ultimate critic: if your controller is wrong, it falls over. There's no cheating. And many tools I'd built up in animation, like trajectory optimization, simulation, and learning controllers, turned out to be exactly what robotics needed, especially as deep reinforcement learning started taking off.

Then there was the sim-to-real problem. Simulation is cheap, safe, and fast, and the real world is none of those things. So the question became: can we train a robot's skills mostly in simulation, the way I'd trained animated characters, and then have them transfer to a physical machine? Our early work on legged robots, learning locomotion in simulation and deploying it on real hardware, was really where my animation background and robotics met. Closing that reality gap felt like a problem my training had prepared me for.

And honestly, the deeper motivation was bigger than any one technique. Animation creates the *illusion* of intelligent movement on a screen. Robotics is about creating *real* intelligent behavior in the physical world. Once I saw that the same ideas could move from pixels to atoms, it was hard to go back.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts optimization in a physics simulator, where movement emerges from the simulated body, physics, and goal, with hand-keyed motion.

r002.rationale: The response says animation tools were useful in robotics and mentions deep reinforcement learning, but does not identify increasing AI use in character-animation research as what made the fields seem closely related.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. It's actually a pretty natural path when you look back on it, even if it didn't feel planned at the time.

When I was doing my PhD, I worked on physics-based character animation. The whole idea there is that instead of hand-animating a character or using motion capture, you build a simulated body with joints and muscles and physics, and then you write a controller that makes it walk, run, swim, whatever. The character has to balance, it has to react to pushes, it has to deal with contact with the ground. If you squint, that's a robot. It's just a robot that lives inside a computer.

And what I found was that the hard problems were the same ones roboticists were struggling with. How do you get a legged system to move in a way that's stable and also looks natural and efficient? How do you handle contact, which is discontinuous and really unfriendly to the math? Even the tools overlapped: optimization, control theory, and later reinforcement learning.

The difference was consequences. In animation, if my controller fell over, I'd get a funny video. In robotics, you break a motor, or worse. For a while that gap kept me on the graphics side, honestly, because it was so much faster to iterate in simulation.

But two things pulled me across. One was personal. I'd spend months making a simulated creature learn to walk, and there was always this nagging feeling: is this real, or is it an artifact of my simulator? I wanted to know whether the ideas held up when physics was no longer something I wrote myself. The second was that around the time I joined Google, the sim-to-real question became tractable. Simulators got better, learning methods got more sample-efficient, and we started to see that policies trained in simulation could actually transfer to real quadrupeds with the right randomization and system identification.

So in a sense I didn't really leave animation. I just moved the character out of the screen and onto the floor. And then the floor started teaching me things the simulator never could, which is what keeps it interesting.

r001.rationale: It contrasts physics-based animation with hand animation, describing simulated bodies governed by joints, muscles, and physics and controllers that produce movement.

r002.rationale: It mentions reinforcement learning among overlapping tools and later learning methods, but does not identify Jie Tan’s increasing use of AI in character-animation research as what made the work seem related to robotics.

astra-6.text:
For me, the connection is movement. In physics-based character animation, you’re trying to make a simulated character move naturally while obeying the laws of physics. That leads to questions about balance, coordination, and control—the same kinds of questions you face in robotics.

What drew me toward robotics was the opportunity to take those ideas into the physical world. In simulation, you control the environment. With a real robot, there’s uncertainty: contact isn’t perfect, sensing isn’t perfect, and things don’t always behave as your model predicts. Making movement work despite all of that felt like a compelling next challenge.

r001.rationale: It describes character animation as producing natural movement in simulation while obeying physical laws, distinguishing it from mere hand-tuning.

r002.rationale: It connects animation to robotics through movement, balance, and control, but does not identify increasing use of AI as the reason.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the connection is that both fields ask how to make a body move intelligently. In physics-based character animation, you’re trying to create motion that obeys physics and looks natural. Robotics adds another challenge: can those ideas work on a real machine, with all the uncertainty of the physical world? That possibility—taking something from simulation and seeing it move in reality—was what drew me toward robotics.

r001.rationale: The response says physics-based animation creates motion that obeys physics and looks natural, but it does not describe mathematical and physical simulation as the method.

r002.rationale: The response attributes Jie Tan’s move toward robotics to applying ideas from simulation in reality; it does not mention increasing use of AI in character-animation research.
